subject: forensic-medicine
title: Medical Ethics: National Medical Commission, Misconduct and Informed Consent

steps.title: Structure and mandate of the National Medical Commission
steps.tx: Established under the National Medical Commission Act of 2019, the **National Medical Commission regulatory authority** serves as the statutory apex body overseeing medical education, licensing, and professional conduct in India, replacing the former Medical Council of India. The commission operates through four specialized autonomous boards that coordinate undergraduate training, postgraduate curricula, medical college accreditation, and professional ethical standards nationwide.
steps.say: The National Medical Commission oversees medical education and ethical licensing in India through four specialized autonomous boards, replacing the Medical Council of India.

rows: Sets MBBS curricula, admissions and college standards
Regulates MD, MS, DM, MCh and fellowship courses
Inspects infrastructure and grants hospital accreditations
Maintains National Register and adjudicates misconduct

steps.title: The Ethics and Medical Registration Board and state councils
steps.tx: The central statutory organ regulating medical morals is the **Ethics and Medical Registration Board**, which compiles the live National Medical Register containing credentials of every registered practitioner in India. While State Medical Councils handle primary state-level registrations and initial disciplinary tribunals, the EMRB acts as the national appellate authority reviewing orders of erasure or suspension passed against doctors.
steps.say: The Ethics Board maintains the National Medical Register and handles ethics appeals, while State Medical Councils manage initial registrations and local disciplinary cases.

nodes.label: State Medical Council disciplinary inquiry and order
Aggrieved doctor appeals to Ethics and Registration Board (EMRB)
Final administrative appeal to National Medical Commission

steps.title: Definition and doctrine of professional misconduct
steps.tx: In medical jurisprudence, statutory **professional misconduct disciplinary liability** encompasses acts or omissions committed by a medical practitioner that are reasonably regarded as disgraceful, dishonourable, or unethical by professional brethren of good repute and competency. Historically termed infamous conduct in a professional respect, this standard penalizes clinicians who violate professional codes, exploit vulnerable patients, or debase the dignity of the healing profession.
steps.say: Professional misconduct refers to actions regarded as disgraceful or dishonourable by competent colleagues, subjecting the practitioner to formal disciplinary penalties.

rows: No immediate loss of license to practice
Erasure for fixed months or years
Prohibits all medical practice during penalty period
Total revocation of license to practice medicine
Prosecution for criminal forgery, fraud, or sexual assault

steps.title: The classic six Ds of infamous conduct
steps.tx: Forensic authorities summarize the primary manifestations of professional misconduct through the **infamous conduct six Ds**, representing classic ethical transgressions that provoke disciplinary erasure. These comprise Adultery (abusing doctor-patient relationships for sexual intimacy), Alcohol (treating patients while intoxicated), Advertising (unsolicited self-promotion), Association (covering unqualified quacks), Dichotomy (commercial fee-splitting or commissions), and Disregard of professional secrecy or issuing false certificates.
steps.say: The six Ds of infamous conduct are adultery, alcohol intoxication on duty, advertising, association with unqualified quacks, dichotomy fee-splitting, and disregarding secrecy.

rows: Violates fiduciary trust and patient vulnerability
Endangers patient life and clinical judgment
Touting for patients or boasting cures
Exposes the public to dangerous pseudo-medical care
Leads to unnecessary interventions and exploitation
Undermines public trust and legal records

steps.title: Issuing false medical certificates and legal liabilities
steps.tx: Issuing a knowingly false, exaggerated, or backdated certificate represents a **fraudulent medical certificate violation** carrying severe disciplinary and criminal sanctions. Medical officers frequently issue certificates regarding illness, fitness, injury severity, disability percentage, age estimation, and cause of death. Under Section 232 BNS, any practitioner issuing a false judicial certificate faces criminal prosecution alongside permanent erasure from the medical register.
steps.say: Signing false, backdated, or fabricated sickness certificates is a serious criminal offence, exposing the doctor to prosecution and permanent loss of medical license.

steps.title: The legal and ethical doctrine of informed consent
steps.tx: Founded on patient autonomy and bodily inviolability, the **informed consent medical doctrine** holds that every competent adult possesses the inviolable legal right to determine what shall be done with their body. A surgical incision or invasive medical intervention performed without valid consent constitutes tortious assault, battery, and medical negligence, exposing the treating practitioner to civil damage claims and criminal charges.
steps.say: Informed consent protects patient autonomy. Every competent adult has the right to decide what happens to their body, making unauthorized surgery a civil battery.

nodes.label: Clinician explains diagnosis and proposed procedure
Discussion of foreseeable risks, alternatives, and prognosis
Verification of patient competence and voluntary choice
Execution of signed, dated informed consent document

steps.title: Essential components of legally valid consent
steps.tx: For consent to hold judicial validity, four **valid informed consent components** must be scrupulously fulfilled before initiating therapy. The consent must be entirely voluntary without coercion, fraud, or misrepresentation; it must be informed, requiring disclosure of diagnosis, risks, and alternatives; it must be specific to the proposed intervention; and it must be granted by a legally competent individual of sound mind.
steps.say: Valid consent requires four things: it must be voluntary, fully informed regarding risks and alternatives, specific to the procedure, and given by a competent adult.

rows: Given freely without duress or undue influence
Threats or emotional manipulation by family/doctor
Nature, purpose, hazards, and alternatives explained
Blanket consent without explaining specific risks
Adult of sound mind (18+ under Contract Act)
Intoxicated, delirious, mentally ill, or minor patient

steps.tx: The form names the operation, lists its risks, and takes a signature because consent is a set of conditions, not a single autograph. Four **valid informed consent components** must be met. Consent has to be voluntary, free of coercion, fraud, and misrepresentation. It has to be informed, with the diagnosis, the risks, and the alternatives disclosed. It has to be specific to the proposed procedure. It has to come from a legally competent person of sound mind.
steps.say: Consent holds only when it is voluntary, when risks, diagnosis, and alternatives have been explained, when it names the actual procedure, and when a competent adult gives it. A signature without those four elements is not valid consent.

steps.title: Age thresholds for consent under Indian law
steps.tx: Indian statutes define specific **age thresholds for medical consent** across clinical settings. Under Section 89 and Section 90 of the Indian Penal Code, an adolescent who has attained twelve years of age can legally consent to a physical clinical examination. However, for consenting to surgical operations, anesthesia, or interventions involving serious risks, the Indian Contract Act mandates the age of majority at eighteen years.
steps.say: Under Indian law, a twelve-year-old can consent to routine physical examination, but surgical operations and invasive risks require an adult aged eighteen or older.

left.title: Age 12 to 18 years
points: Can consent to routine clinical examination
Parental consent required for major surgery
Protected under POCSO Act below 18 years

right.title: Age 18 years and above
points: Full legal capacity to consent to surgery
Can donate blood and postmortem organs

steps.title: Therapeutic privilege and emergency exceptions to consent
steps.tx: Under exceptional circumstances, the **therapeutic privilege clinical doctrine** allows a physician to withhold specific distressing diagnostic or prognostic details if direct disclosure would psychologically destabilize a fragile patient, precipitating immediate suicide or fatal cardiac arrest. However, this exception cannot be exploited for administrative convenience, and full disclosure must always be provided to close family guardians.
steps.say: Therapeutic privilege allows doctors to withhold distressing information only if disclosure would cause psychological collapse, with full facts given to the family.

nodes.label: Severe prognosis or malignant diagnosis identified
Judicious therapeutic withholding of devastating details
Full disclosure and consent obtained from next of kin
